newsitem.title: BURMA: Rangoon mosque vandalised by Buddhist monks.
newsitem.headline: Rangoon mosque vandalised by Buddhist monks.

text.p: Religious unrest spread to the Burmese capital on Saturday as a group of about 50 Buddhist monks vandalised a Moslem mosque in the northeastern quarter of Rangoon, witnesses said.
The monks threw stones and used sticks to hit scaffolding around the building and smash its windows.
They dispersed just before police arrived 20 minutes later at the scene, about 10 km (six miles) from downtown Rangoon.
Neither police nor military government spokesmen were available for comment.

The unrest was the first of its kind in the capital, and came soon after Buddhist-Moslem strife broke out in Burma's second city Mandalay, where an 8p.m. to 4 a.m. curfew has been in force since last weekend.
Buddhist monks in Mandalay last weekend rioted and attacked mosques there after a report that a young Buddhist girl had been raped by a Moslem man, government sources and diplomats said.
"About 50 monks arrived in cars at the mosque in Kanbe, where they struck the mosque with sticks and stones," one witness said.
No arrests were made, but tight security was imposed in the area, witnesses added.
Monks played a key role in pro-democracy uprisings from 1988-1990 and many were arrested after refusing to perform religious services for soldiers and their families then.
Burma is about 90 percent Buddhist and many of the country's monks live in Mandalay.
Conflicting reports have emerged on the Mandalay unrest with some diplomats saying they had heard one monk died after troops shot over the heads of protesting monks on Monday.
The ruling military State Law and Order Restoration Council (SLORC) has denied the reports and claims that the unrest was spreading to other areas but acknowledged that a curfew remains in Mandalay.
Besides a curfew, authorities have also banned meetings of over five poeple in some townships in Mandalay.

Monks associated with exiled student groups based at the Burma-Thai border have claimed that 15 monks had been arrested and jailed after the unrest and some others were being detained or awaiting trial in prisons.
On Saturday, a senior SLORC official made Burma's first official but veiled reference to the troubles in Mandalay.
The powerful Secretary Two of the SLORC, Lieutenant General Tin Oo accused traitors at home and "neo-colonialists" abroad of orchestrating recent racial and religious riots.
"Internal traitors, joining with neo-colonialists, are instigating racial and religious conflicts to mar already-restored community peace and tranquility," he said in the offcial media
